extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers responsible for assessing submissions to ACM CHI 2022 (HCI conference)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reviewing and recommending decisions on submissions to the ACM CHI 2022 conference, emphasizing contribution to HCI, appropriate paper length, novelty/prior-publication rules, transparency, and review quality. Intended to guide ACs/PCs and external reviewers in producing useful, consistent reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary criterion — contribution to HCI
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this submission provide a strong contribution to the field of HCI? In all cases, a CHI paper must break new ground and make an original research contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember there are many ways a paper can make a contribution to HCI; review the paper appropriately for the type of contribution. See 'Contributions to CHI', 'Selecting a Subcommittee', and the 'Guide to a Successful Submission' for lists and associated criteria. Lack of contribution (i.e., not breaking new ground) is grounds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate according to contribution type
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many ways a paper can make a contribution to HCI; reviewers should evaluate a submission appropriately given its contribution type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the lists in 'Selecting a Subcommittee' to recognize contribution types and use the 'Guide to a Successful Submission' for criteria specific to those contribution types. Do not apply a one-size-fits-all standard — adapt expectations (e.g., evaluation rigor, theoretical contribution, design insight) to what the paper claims to contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper length must be commensurate with contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper length should be commensurate with the paper’s contribution. CHI 2022 has no strict page limits, but length should match the depth and scope of the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical submissions are expected to be ~7,000–8,000 words (excluding references and figure/table captions). Significantly longer or shorter submissions will receive extra scrutiny. Papers will be perceived as too long if repetitive or verbose; too short if they omit important details, neglect relevant prior art, or tamper with formatting rules to save page count. Papers whose lengths are incommensurate with their contributions will be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and conciseness of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and conciseness of writing are vital to high-quality submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though there's no strict page limit, authors are encouraged to be concise. Repetition and verbosity are negative indicators. If important details are omitted because the paper is too short, that is also a negative. Consider clarity when judging the paper’s ability to communicate its contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and prior-publication policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Content appearing at CHI should be new and groundbreaking; material previously published in widely disseminated archival publications should not be republished unless significantly revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to ACM Policy on Pre-Publication Evaluation and ACM Policy on Prior Publication and Simultaneous Submissions. Roughly, a significant revision would contain more than 25% new content (new insights, new results) and significantly amplify or clarify the original material — these are subjective assessments for reviewers/committee. Exceptions: translation into English of previously published non-English work (typically with the original author involved) is allowed if declared in the abstract. Non-archival venues (workshop presentations, posters, Late-Breaking Work) do not count as prior publication. Work published independently after the CHI submission was made should not count against an author if the author could not have known about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication as a valid contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive replication of other researchers’ work can be a significant contribution to HCI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication is allowed and valued; however, submitted replication work must include sufficient information to allow future replications. Efforts to include complete, well-organized supplementary material (software, analysis code, data) facilitating replication should be rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in reporting results
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency in the way research results are reported can be a ground to doubt the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper reports methods, analyses, and results transparently enough for readers to judge and for future replication. See the 'Transparency' section in the 'Guide to a Successful Submission' for discussion of transparency expectations in different contribution types. When transparency is lacking, this weakens claims of contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not penalize topic mismatch with subcommittee
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not judge the paper by how well it fits the subcommittee theme(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many papers will not cleanly fit a particular subcommittee; authors should not be penalized for this. Evaluate the paper by its own quality and contribution. Any topic is valid as long as it fits within the interests of a reasonable fraction of the overall CHI audience. Remember subcommittee organization is for reviewer matching and handling volume, not for defining absolute topical merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation must match written appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers decide the overall recommendation (Accept with minor revisions, Revise and Resubmit, and Reject) on each submission and must provide a written appraisal that matches their recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the written review justifies the chosen recommendation; short unexplained recommendations (especially short positive reviews) are unhelpful. A high-quality review typically is about a page of written text. Detailed feedback is expected even when the reviewer likes the paper; short positive reviews without justification create difficulties in PC discussions and are discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality expectations and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality reviews are detailed and constructive; very short reviews are frustrating and undermine the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for about a page of written text. Provide specific critiques, evidence for claims (e.g., why contribution is/ is not sufficient), suggestions for improvement, and point-to-point commentary on major weaknesses. Avoid one-line endorsements or terse negative comments without justification. Explicitly call out examples of problematic practices to justify critiques (e.g., missing prior work, insufficient methodological detail, formatting tampering).
